newsitem.title: USA: White House says best of NAFTA yet to come.
newsitem.headline: White House says best of NAFTA yet to come.

text.p: White House officials said Friday the first three years of the North American Free Trade Agreement have been good for the nation's economy and the best was yet to come.

In a report to Congress on the trade pact, which links the United States, Canada and Mexico in a trading bloc, the administration said it has had a "modest positive" impact on the economy since it went into effect in January 1994.

"There will be another 12 years of market opening measures taken by Mexico," U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said at a news conference. "We are only in the third year of a 15-year agreement. We expect to see the positive trends we see here continue."

The report to Congress, required by law, stressed some of the more positive effects the pact has had on trade among the NAFTA partners and on U.S. businesses such as autos, food, chemicals, electronics, phone equipment and textiles.
But critics said it glossed over some of the harmful effects on workers.

"In this booming economy, while stockholders and corporate executives are making record profits, the real wages of working people in America are at a standsill. For Mexican workers, wages have fallen up to 40 percent," Teamsters union President Ron Carey said in a statement.

"Working familes have been harmed in many other ways," he added. "NAFTA threatens food and highway safety. It has opened a new pipeline for drugs into our neighbourhoods and schools. And it has increased pollution along the border."
Critics also said the United States is running trade deficits with its NAFTA partners and argued that a trade surplus with Mexico before the agreement has fallen to a $16 billion deficit.
They also said that the jobs promised by the administration when it was trying to convince Congress to vote for NAFTA in 1993 have not materialised.

But White House economic adviser Gene Sperling said that the number of jobs from trade with Mexico and Canada had risen by 311,000 after NAFTA. He also said he disagreed that wages were at a standstill, saying family and per capita income have risen in recent years.

Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said NAFTA helped Mexico recover more quickly from its 1995 financial crisis. He also said that as the Mexican economy recovers from the recession caused by the crisis, one of the challenges facing the government is to be sure the benefits are shared by all.
"One of their challenges as they go forward is to see that that prosperity is spread through society," Rubin said.
Barshefsky said the U.S. trade deficit was due mostly to robust domestic growth during a period of slow growth in Canada and recession in Mexico.

The report is expected to lay the groundwork for a push by President Clinton later this year for new trade negotiation authority that would allow Barshefsky to negotiate an expansion of NAFTA to include Chile without fear the agreement will be later changed by Congress.
Barshefsky said the so-called fast-track trade negotiation authority was needed for a range of upcoming trade talks. But critics of NAFTA are urging Congress to reject new fast-track authority.
"NAFTA's fast-track must be stopped in its tracks," Representative Bob Barr, a Georgia Republican, said. "Congress should move deliberately to derail this southbound train."
